analysis.one_liner: Caps U.S. greenhouse gas emissions under a declining tradeable permit system through 2050.
analysis.headline: The Senate's leading climate bill cleared the Environment and Public Works Committee and was placed on the Senate calendar in May 2008, but the Senate never voted on it before the Congress ended in January 2009.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would set a nationwide limit on greenhouse gas pollution, starting in 2012 and falling every year until 2050, so that total allowed emissions drop to roughly 30% of today's level. Power plants, factories, and producers and importers of fossil fuels would have to hold one government-issued permit for every ton they emit, and could buy, sell, or bank those permits. The bill also directs where the permits go: some are auctioned to fund clean energy, low-income energy bill help, and worker retraining, while many are given free to the very utilities and industries being regulated, plus states, farmers, and adaptation programs.
analysis.who_benefits: Everyone exposed to climate damage benefits from the declining cap. Low- and middle-income energy consumers get help with bills through the Energy Assistance Fund (LIHEAP, weatherization, rural assistance), workers get a federal training program for low-carbon energy jobs, states get allowances to fund transit, efficiency, and relief for energy-intensive industries, and clean-energy industries get auction proceeds for zero- and low-carbon power, advanced coal with carbon capture, cellulosic fuels, and advanced vehicle manufacturing. Covered utilities, fuel producers, and heavy industry also benefit in the early years, because the bill allocates most allowances free of charge to them rather than auctioning everything.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Energy consumers, workers, clean-energy firms — and regulated utilities

how_it_helps.text: Sets a nationwide emissions cap that starts at 5,200 million allowances in 2012 and declines each year to 1,560 million in 2050 — a cut of about 70% — covering power plants, industrial facilities, and producers or importers of fossil-based fuels and chemicals.

Creates an Energy Assistance Fund whose money goes to the Low Income Home Energy Assistance Program, the Weatherization Assistance Program for Low-Income Persons, and rural energy assistance, to cushion higher energy bills for low- and middle-income households.

Establishes a Climate Change Worker Training Program run by the Secretary of Labor to train workers for jobs in low-carbon energy, sustainable energy, and energy efficiency, with grants to states and partnerships with labor organizations.

Allocates 9% of allowances to electricity providers and 2% to natural gas distribution companies, whose proceeds must be used to mitigate economic impacts on low- and middle-income energy consumers and promote efficiency — and bars them from using the money for usage-based rebates.

Gives states 5% of allowances each year for low-income energy consumer relief, energy efficiency, public transit and passenger rail, adaptation to local climate impacts, and relief for energy-intensive industries, among other uses.
Requires the SEC to direct public companies to disclose material climate-related risks to investors.
Creates a federal greenhouse gas registry with verified, publicly posted emissions data and penalties of up to $25,000 per day for noncompliance.

Requires an international reserve allowance program starting in 2019 for imports from countries without comparable emission limits, with proceeds helping disadvantaged communities abroad adapt to climate change.

analysis.who_pays: Covered fossil-energy producers and heavy industry bear the compliance cost of holding permits for every ton emitted, and electric utilities will pass allowance costs through to household and business electricity rates. Consumers as a whole pay more for energy — the bill's cost-relief mechanisms exist precisely because of that. In addition, because a large share of allowances is handed out free to covered companies rather than auctioned, some of the program's monetary value becomes a gift to the regulated firms instead of revenue for public purposes; the bill's free allocations also reward firms that lobbied hardest for their share.
analysis.who_pays_short: Fossil-fuel producers, heavy industry, and energy consumers

drawbacks.text: Most allowances in the early years are given free to covered power plants, fuel producers, and energy-intensive manufacturers rather than auctioned, so a large share of the program's value flows to the regulated companies; consumers still face higher energy prices, and the companies profit from both.

Covered facilities can meet up to 15% of their obligation with domestic offsets, up to 15% with foreign market allowances, and up to 15% by borrowing future allowances at interest — escape valves that let real domestic emissions run higher than the headline cap in any given year.

The bill's own enforcement gap shows in its design: facilities that fail to submit allowances pay a penalty and must offset excess emissions the following year, meaning an underperforming cap produces paper penalties rather than immediate emission cuts.

A Carbon Market Efficiency Board can loosen the program if it finds the allowance market is harming the economy — expanding borrowing, increasing foreign and offset allowances, or expanding the total allowance quantity — giving an unelected board authority to soften the cap.
Burning fossil fuels will cost more under the cap, and while assistance targets low-income households, middle-income households and energy-intensive businesses still absorb higher costs.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core benefit — a legally binding, decades-long decline in U.S. greenhouse gas emissions — is large and the mechanism is genuinely enforceable, with verified reporting and penalties. But the design is generous to the regulated industries: early free allocations and broad escape valves (offsets, international credits, borrowing, and a cost-relief board) mean more of the cap's monetary value goes to utilities and fuel producers, and less domestic reduction is guaranteed in any given year, than a simpler auction-based system would deliver. For ordinary households, the bill is a real climate protection paid for partly through higher energy bills, with targeted relief for the poorest — a trade-off many analysts judged uneven in who captures the money.

outcome.mechanism: The Senate Environment and Public Works Committee approved and reported the bill, and it sat on the Senate's legislative calendar, but the full Senate never took a final vote on it; in June 2008 a companion vehicle for the same proposal failed a cloture vote — the procedural step needing 60 senators to cut off debate — and the 110th Congress ended in January 2009 with the bill still pending.

narrative.text: S. 2191 was introduced in the Senate on October 18, 2007 by Senator Lieberman with Senator Warner and ten other original cosponsors, and was read twice and referred to the Committee on Environment and Public Works.
A subcommittee held hearings in October 2007 and approved the bill for full committee consideration, and the full committee held hearings in November 2007.
On December 5, 2007 the committee ordered the bill reported favorably with an amendment in the nature of a substitute.
On May 20, 2008 the committee reported the bill with an amendment, with a written report (No. 110-337) and minority views filed by committee Republicans.
The bill was placed on the Senate Legislative Calendar under General Orders (Calendar No. 740) on May 20, 2008 — its last action in the 110th Congress.
The bill never received a floor vote in the Senate, and the 110th Congress ended on January 3, 2009 with the bill still pending on the calendar.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Covered utilities, coal and oil interests, and other emitters came out ahead: no federal emissions cap ever took effect, so they avoided the compliance costs the bill would have imposed for two more years. The many firms and farmers that had been positioning for the new allowance and offset markets, and the households the bill would have assisted, got nothing.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Fossil-energy producers; the emissions cap never took effect

for.role: Lead sponsor, Senate Environment and Public Works Committee
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and guided it through subcommittee and full committee markup to a favorable report.

for.name: Sen. John Warner
for.what_they_did: Co-introduced the bill as the ranking Republican author, giving it bipartisan sponsorship.

for.name: Sen. Barbara Boxer
for.role: Chair, Senate Environment and Public Works Committee
for.what_they_did: Chaired the hearings and markup and reported the bill to the Senate with an amendment on May 20, 2008.

for.name: Eleven Senate cosponsors
for.what_they_did: Signed on as cosponsors, including Democrats Harkin, Cardin, Klobuchar, Casey, Nelson, Wyden, and Schumer and Republicans Coleman, Dole, and Collins.

against.name: Senate Republicans
against.what_they_did: Opposed bringing the bill to a final vote; in June 2008 the Senate debated a companion vehicle and the bloc sustained a filibuster, and the motion to cut off debate failed to reach the 60 votes needed.

against.name: Environment and Public Works Committee Republicans
against.role: Minority members of the reporting committee
against.what_they_did: Filed minority views alongside the May 20, 2008 committee report, signaling opposition to the bill as reported.

against.name: U.S. Chamber of Commerce and allied business groups
against.what_they_did: Ran a public campaign against the cap-and-trade framework as an economy-wide cost, pressuring senators to oppose floor consideration.

against.name: President George W. Bush
against.what_they_did: Publicly opposed cap-and-trade legislation that would raise energy costs, discouraging Senate Republicans from supporting floor action.

sides.party_line_note: The bill began as genuine bipartisan work — an independent and a Republican as lead authors, with 11 cosponsors split 4 Republicans and 7 Democrats — but committee Republicans filed minority views on the reported bill and Senate Republicans as a bloc kept a final vote from ever happening.

industries.industry: Coal-fired electric utilities and power companies
industries.note: The bill caps their emissions but hands them large free allocations of allowances in the early years and transition assistance through 2029, making them the main distribution channel for the program's value to electricity consumers. Households still pay higher power rates as allowance costs pass through, with a portion offset by low- and middle-income assistance.

A declining emissions cap and a per-ton permit cost directly shrink demand for coal, the most carbon-intensive fuel; the bill softens the blow with bonus allowances for carbon capture projects and advanced coal technology funding, but the industry's long-term revenue under the bill is smaller than under no bill — which is why its loss is the public's gain.

industries.industry: Oil and gas producers and refiners
industries.note: Producers and importers of petroleum-based fuels are covered entities that must hold allowances for every ton their fuels will emit, raising fuel costs, though they also receive transition assistance allowances through 2029. Motorists pay more at the pump under the cap; the bill partly offsets this through energy assistance funds.

Auction proceeds fund deployment of zero- and low-carbon generation, cellulosic biofuels, and carbon capture demonstration projects, and utilities get incentives to buy efficient products. The bill creates a large, funded market for these firms' products alongside the public's interest in cleaner power.

The bill funds up to 30% of the cost of reequipping plants to build electric, hybrid, fuel-cell, and advanced diesel vehicles and components — paid out of auction proceeds. Manufacturers out of fuel-economy compliance are barred from receiving awards.

Farmers, ranchers, and foresters can earn offset allowances for sequestration and methane projects — up to 15% of the cap's compliance demand — and USDA gets 5% of allowances plus an outreach program to help landowners market them. This creates a new revenue stream for landowners, with the quality of offsets policed by verification and reversal rules.

The bill creates a national market in emission allowances and explicitly bars restricting purchases to regulated facilities, opening trading to financial firms and speculators. Trading helps lower compliance costs, but a speculative market also concentrates profit and introduces price risk that the bill addresses with its cost-relief board.

These firms face allowance costs for their own emissions but receive transition assistance allowances through 2029 and state-level allowances earmarked to mitigate their competitive disadvantage against countries without emission limits.
